first.rationale: Two of the three current problems are activation (-6%) and onboarding completion (-4%), which are exactly the funnel stages that memory_31 (signup field reduction lifting SMB first-week activation) and memory_86 (shorter onboarding lifting completion and time-to-value) address; onboarding simplification is the single lever that plausibly moves both at once, and its gains are structural rather than purchased, which fits the sustainable-qualified-revenue objective. I am deliberately not choosing promotional_pricing despite the competitor's entry pricing: memory_73 records that it bought acquisition at the cost of a material 30-day retention drop and explicitly warns against generalizing it, so it would trade long-term qualified revenue for a short-term defensive win. Referral incentive (memory_57) is sound but targets established customers, not the failing top-of-funnel; enterprise_sales_assist (memory_44) is a different segment entirely and does not touch the observed declines. I spend the verification budget on memory_31 and memory_86 because they are the two memories my chosen action rests on, and both are consolidated summaries whose original records I want to check for scope and durability caveats: memory_31 is the oldest (day 12) and may predate the current product; memory_86 says 'completion rates and time-to-value' but consolidation may have dropped whether the lift persisted past week one or whether looser signup admitted lower-quality accounts. If either source record shows the lift was measured only on a proxy metric, or that reduced friction degraded lead quality or downstream retention, I will fall back to activation_messaging (memory_91), which addresses the larger of the two declines with an in-product change that does not alter who gets in the door. Downstream value risk is real and flagged: removing signup friction can raise activation counts while lowering the qualified-revenue value of each account, the same shape of failure memory_73 documents, so this runs as a standard experiment with retention and lead-quality guardrails and a qualified-revenue readout rather than an activation-only readout. My confidence rests on inherited consolidated summaries, not re-verified primary data, and I am treating that as provisional until the archive returns.

final.rationale: Both source records came back confirmed, and they resolve the specific worry I had. exp_86 (shortened onboarding) shows completion +13%, time-to-value -2.1 days, and 30-day retention +3% — the lift is not a friction-removal illusion, since retention moved the right way, which is exactly the failure mode I was checking for. exp_31 (signup simplification) also holds, with activation +9% and qualified revenue +4%, but carries a small retention drag (-1%) and is explicitly SMB-only, not replicated on other segments. So I commit the slot to simplify_onboarding, weighting the onboarding-flow intervention (exp_86) as the primary design since it is the cleaner evidence, applies across self-serve rather than one segment, and directly targets onboarding completion (-4%) while plausibly relieving activation (-6%) through faster time-to-value. Where the two overlap I lean on exp_86's flow-shortening rather than aggressive signup-field stripping, because the field-stripping variant is where the retention cost and the segment restriction live. I am still declining promotional_pricing as the competitive response: memory_73 records material 30-day retention loss and an explicit warning not to generalize it, and buying back price-sensitive SMB accounts that churn in a month is directly opposed to sustainable long-term qualified revenue. Referral (memory_57) targets existing customers and enterprise_sales_assist (memory_44) targets a segment showing no decline; neither addresses this quarter's actual leak. Residual uncertainty I am not papering over: neither source record was run under competitor price pressure, so the observed declines may be partly demand-mix rather than funnel friction, and an onboarding fix would then underdeliver; exp_31's cross-segment non-replication also means I should not assume the effect transfers to mid-market or enterprise. Guardrails accordingly: read out on 30-day retention and qualified revenue per account, not activation counts alone, and monitor whether any new-account inflow is disproportionately price-sensitive churn-risk. If retention or per-account qualified revenue degrades, activation_messaging (memory_91) is the fallback for the next slot, since it lifts engagement without changing who enters the funnel.
